description: We are a Wolfpack team from North Carolina State University tackling Health Monitoring Systems for Astronauts in space challenge. Our app tracks crew vitals and check-ins, learns each person's baseline, flags changes and suggests next steps.
summary: SpacePack is health monitoring software that allows astronauts to check their own health at a glance, without being well versed in medical knowledge. It combines live readings from a wearable device with environmental readings from the cabin to track heart rate, heart rate variability, blood oxygen, breathing rate and more. Statuses are shown on almost every page and tell the user if immediate medical attention is needed. The software gives advice for handling sudden problems and the option to involve a crewmate or the flight surgeon. We included personal touches to make the software feel more personal for each user, including a place for photos from home and a daily journal for physical and mental notes.
details:
What it does

SpacePack is a web app. The main screen shows a clickable body figure with the status of each body system, any alerts, and the day's health routine. Other screens show live vitals, trends over time, a daily check-in, guided measurements, a private journal and mission settings.

How it works

The app stores every reading and checks it against clear rules. It compares readings with safe limits and with the astronaut's own baseline, and it looks for slow drift over several days. When something is off, it raises an alert with plain advice. Each alert has three help steps: handle it yourself, tell a crewmate, or contact the flight surgeon.

The analysis changes with the mission. Radiation alert levels are different for low Earth orbit, the Moon and Mars, because radiation is stronger farther from Earth. A weekly vision check looks for eye changes that long spaceflight can cause.

Benefits and impact

Astronauts are not doctors. SpacePack explains what each number means, why space affects it, what is normal, and what to do if it is off. Our goal is earlier detection and more independence for crews on long missions.

Creativity

- The app rewards healthy habits, never the health numbers. A bad day earns the same points as a good day, so nobody hides symptoms.

- A rocket fuels up as daily tasks get done, and astronauts rise through ranks from Cadet to Commander.

- The look of the app changes with the mission's location, using real NASA photos.

- Astronauts can add photos from home to lift their mood.

- Status always uses a colour, an icon and a word, so it works for colour-blind users.

Tools

We used Python and FastAPI for the backend, and TypeScript and React for the website. A built-in simulator creates healthy, mixed or unwell data for the demo.

What we considered

Privacy, honest self-reporting, accessibility, communication delay, and being easy to read under stress.

NASA and partner resources

We used NASA's Human Research Program pages on the 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight and the Risks of Human Spaceflight, and the Canadian Space Agency's page on monitoring radiation for astronaut health. The background photos are from NASA's image library.
